label: Ruth — Complete
summary_plain: Ruth is a Mo'avite woman who clings to her mother-in-law Na'omi after the death of their husbands. She says: Where you go I will go. Where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your Creator my Creator. Ruth gleans in the fields of Bo'az, a relative of Na'omi's husband. Bo'az acts as the kinsman redeemer. Ruth and Bo'az marry. Their son Oved is the father of Yishai, the father of Dawid. Ruth the Mo'avite is in the direct lineage of King Dawid.
summary_scholarly: Ruth is preserved in DSS fragments (4QRuth-a, 4QRuth-b) and in the Orit Ge'ez. The text establishes that the Davidic royal lineage includes a non-Israelite woman — a Mo'avite. The kinsman-redeemer (go'el) framework is central to covenant law: the obligation to redeem family property and preserve a deceased relative's name through levirate marriage. Bo'az fulfills this obligation publicly at the gate.

key_terms.definition: A Moavite woman who chooses to remain with her mother-in-law Naomi after the death of her husband, declaring loyalty to Naomi's people and to YHWH. Her story is set in the days of the shofetim (judges).

The Bethlehemite woman who loses her husband and two sons in Moav; returns to Beit-Lekhem with Rut; calls herself 'Mara' (bitter) on her return; is ultimately restored through Rut's loyalty and Boaz's redemption.

Rut 1:16 — Rut's declaration to Naomi: 'Where you go I will go; where you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people and your YHWH my YHWH.' One of the most celebrated loyalty declarations in the Hebrew covenant tradition.
A man of Beit-Lekhem from the clan of Elimelekh, Naomi's deceased husband; a person of standing (gibbor khayil); becomes Rut's kinsman-redeemer, marrying her and restoring the family line.

The Hebrew legal institution where a close male relative has the right and responsibility to redeem a family member's property or widow; central to the plot of Rut — Boaz acts as go'el for Naomi and Rut, restoring Elimelekh's land and lineage.

The practice reflected in Rut (adjacent to Deuteronomy 25 levirate law) where a kinsman marries a widow to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance; the nearer kinsman declines, leaving Boaz free to act as go'el.

Rut 3: Naomi instructs Rut to uncover Boaz's feet and lie down at the threshing floor; Boaz wakes and Rut asks him to spread his covering (wing) over her as go'el — a legal appeal to kinsman-redemption using the same 'wing' language as YHWH's redemption (2:12).

Naomi's other daughter-in-law, also a Moavite; weeps and kisses Naomi when urged to return to her people, then does return — contrasted with Rut who chooses to stay. Orpah is not condemned; the contrast highlights the extraordinary nature of Rut's loyalty.

Rut 4:17-22: Rut bears a son named Oved; he is the father of Yishai; Yishai is the father of David. The genealogy at the book's end reveals that the Moavite Rut is in the direct ancestral line of the Davidic covenant.

Hebrew word for covenant loyalty, loving-kindness, faithful love; used three times in Rut to describe both Rut's loyalty to Naomi and YHWH's covenant faithfulness. Khesed is the theological center of the book.

faq.question: Why is Rut, a Moavite, the central hero of a book in the Hebrew covenant tradition?
faq.answer: Rut demonstrates that covenant loyalty (khesed) is not determined by ethnicity but by faithfulness to YHWH and to the covenant community. Her declaration — 'your people shall be my people and your YHWH my YHWH' — is a full covenant commitment. The book presents her as a model of khesed that surpasses what is required, and YHWH rewards her accordingly. The Davidic lineage running through Rut shows that YHWH works through unexpected paths.

faq.question: What is the go'el institution and how does it work in Rut?
faq.answer: The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) is a close male relative responsible for redeeming family land, freeing enslaved relatives, or marrying a deceased kinsman's widow to continue the family name. In Rut, Naomi's husband Elimelekh had a nearer kinsman who had first right of redemption — but he declines (4:6) because taking Rut's hand would complicate his own inheritance. This clears the path for Boaz to act as go'el, completing the legal ceremony at the city gate with ten elders (4:1-12).

faq.question: What is the significance of Rut's request in 3:9?
faq.answer: Rut's request — 'Spread your wing over your servant, for you are a go'el' — echoes Boaz's earlier blessing (2:12) where he said YHWH would reward her for coming under YHWH's wings for refuge. Rut is now asking Boaz to be the human embodiment of YHWH's protective wing through the go'el institution. The same Hebrew word for wing/covering (kanaf) connects YHWH's protection and Boaz's covenant responsibility — Rut is claiming both simultaneously.

faq.question: What is Khesed and why is it the theological center of Rut?
faq.answer: Khesed is covenant loyalty — faithful love that goes beyond what is strictly required, persisting through difficulty. Naomi invokes it in 1:8: 'May YHWH deal khesed with you as you have dealt with the dead and with me.' Boaz praises Rut's khesed in 3:10. YHWH is the source of khesed, and both Rut and Boaz model it in human form. The whole story is a demonstration that khesed — divine and human — is the engine of covenant restoration.

faq.question: What does the ending genealogy of Rut reveal?
faq.answer: Rut 4:17-22 traces the lineage from Perez through ten generations to David. Oved, born of Rut and Boaz, is the grandfather of David. This genealogy transforms the whole story: what appears to be a small personal story of loyalty and loss in a Moavite field is actually part of the larger covenant story leading to the Davidic covenant. YHWH works through the margins — a widowed Moavite woman — to bring about covenant history.

faq.question: What does the contrast between Rut and Orpah teach?
faq.answer: Orpah is not condemned — she weeps, she loved Naomi, and she followed the socially expected path of returning to her family after widowhood. Rut's choice is extraordinary precisely because Orpah represents the normal and understandable option. The contrast highlights that Rut's covenant loyalty is voluntary, not compelled — she chose YHWH and the covenant community when she had every reasonable option to leave. This voluntary covenant commitment is exactly what makes her story a model.

faq.question: How does the book of Rut position itself within the larger Hebrew narrative?
faq.answer: Rut opens in the days of the shofetim (judges) — a period described in Shofetim as characterized by everyone doing what was right in their own eyes. The book of Rut is a counternarrative: in the same period, ordinary people practiced extraordinary khesed. It ends with the genealogy of David, connecting directly to the beginning of the Shemu'el/Melakhim narrative. Rut is the bridge from the judges period to the Davidic covenant.

faq.question: What does Rut 1:16-17 teach about covenant commitment?
faq.answer: Rut's declaration is not just a loyalty pledge to Naomi personally — it is a full covenant commitment: people, place, YHWH, and even death and burial. 'Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried.' This covers every dimension of covenant identity: community, land, deity, and the final resting place. Rut is not requesting immigrant status — she is fully joining the covenant community. Her words have been used ever since in Jewish conversion contexts precisely because they represent total covenant allegiance.

faq.question: Why does Naomi call herself Mara (bitter)?
faq.answer: Naomi returns to Beit-Lekhem after losing her husband Elimelekh and both sons. She says: 'I went away full and YHWH has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi (pleasant) when YHWH has afflicted me?' (1:21). This honest lament echoes Iyov's honesty with YHWH. Naomi does not pretend faith she doesn't feel — she names the bitterness directly. The book's arc will restore her to fullness, but she must first be allowed to name the loss.

faq.question: What covenant legal elements appear in the city gate scene of Rut 4?
faq.answer: Rut 4:1-12 follows the formal legal process: Boaz assembles ten elders as witnesses at the city gate (the legal forum in ancient Hebrew towns); the nearer kinsman is invited to redeem; he initially agrees but withdraws when he learns Rut is part of the transaction; he symbolically removes his sandal (the legal sign of declining the levirate/go'el obligation, related to Devarim 25:9); and Boaz formally declares his redemption of both the land and Rut before all the witnesses. The legal precision of the scene reflects functioning covenant law.
